content: Revolutions per minute (abbreviated as rpm, RPM, r/min, or r·min⁻¹) is a unit of frequency that quantifies the number of complete rotations made around a fixed axis in one minute. It is primarily used to measure the rotational speed or angular velocity of mechanical components. Standards organizations generally recommend the symbol r/min for consistency with other unit symbols, though this is not universally enforced. For instance, in French, the term tr/min (tours par minute) is commonly used. The corresponding unit in the International System of Units (SI) is the hertz (Hz), and angular velocity in SI is often expressed in radians per second (rad·s⁻¹). To convert revolutions per minute to hertz, divide the value by 60. Examples of Rotational Speeds: 1. Disc or tape-like recording media: The rotational speed of the medium under the read head is typically specified in r/min. 2. Modern dental drills: These can achieve rotational speeds of up to 500,000 r/min (8 kHz). 3. Second hand of an analogue clock: This rotates at a speed of 1 r/min. 4. CD-ROM drives: Their maximum rotational speeds are rated in multiples of a base speed, though they do not maintain constant read speeds across most disc formats. 5. DVD players: These typically read discs at a constant linear rate, with speeds also given in multiples of a base speed. 6. Washing machine drums: During spin cycles, these can rotate at speeds ranging from 500 to 2,000 r/min (8–33 Hz). 7. Automobile engines: These generally operate between 700 and 7,000 r/min (12–120 Hz), though some high-performance engines can reach up to 11,000 r/min (180 Hz). 8. Piston aircraft engines: These typically rotate at speeds between 2,000 and 3,000 r/min (30–50 Hz). 9. Computer hard drives: Common rotational speeds are 5,400 or 7,200 r/min (90 or 120 Hz) for drives with ATA or SATA interfaces, while high-performance drives can reach 10,000 or 15,000 r/min (160 or 250 Hz) with SATA, SCSI, or Fibre Channel interfaces. 10. Formula One racing car engines: These can achieve rotational speeds of up to 19,000 r/min (320 Hz) under certain conditions. 11. Gas centrifuges for uranium enrichment: These can spin at speeds of 90,000 r/min (1,500 Hz) or higher. 12. Gas turbine engines: These typically operate at tens of thousands of r/min. 13. JetCat model aircraft turbines: These can exceed 100,000 r/min (1,700 Hz), with the fastest reaching 165,000 r/min (2,750 Hz). 14. Electromechanical batteries (EMBs): These operate in the range of 60,000–200,000 r/min (1–3 kHz) using a passively magnetically levitated flywheel in a vacuum. The flywheel material is chosen not for its density but for its ability to safely disintegrate at surface speeds approximately seven times the speed of sound. 15. Turbochargers: These can reach speeds of 290,000 r/min (4,800 Hz), with common operating ranges between 80,000 and 200,000 r/min (1–3 kHz).
